sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax in Geauga County?
sections.html:
Three county offices in Chardon share the work. The County Auditor appraises and assesses every parcel, the County Treasurer sends bills and takes payment, and the Board of Revision hears value complaints.

The Board of Revision is made up of the Auditor, who serves as its permanent secretary, the president of the County Commissioners and the Treasurer. The Auditor's office is at 231 Main Street, Suite 1-A, Chardon, Ohio 44024, with a real estate direct line of (440) 279-1617 and a main line of (440) 279-1600.

sections.h2: When are Geauga County property taxes billed and due?
sections.html:
Geauga County bills the first half in January and the second half in June. Both halves are always due on the second Wednesday of February and the second Wednesday of July, according to the Auditor's property search page.

The Treasurer sends tax bills only by regular mail, and the Auditor's portal warns that any text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent. The portal also carries a yearly tax calendar for the exact dates.

  • Tax bills come from the Treasurer, not from the Auditor.
  • Payment by text message is a scam and should be deleted.
  • Ask the Treasurer for a payoff on a specific parcel before closing.

sections.h2: How many parcels does the Geauga County Auditor value?
sections.html:
On January 1, 2026 the Auditor's portal counted 52,207 parcels in Geauga County. The Auditor's real estate page says the office must see that every parcel and the buildings on it are fairly and uniformly appraised.

The county has 33 taxing districts, so two houses with the same value can carry different bills depending on the township, village and school district they sit in.

sections.h2: How often are Geauga County values updated?
sections.html:
Ohio law requires a general reappraisal of all real property every six years, with an update in the third year. The Auditor's appraisal office carries out the sexennial reappraisals, the triennial updates and annual new construction valuations, and its field appraisers visit every property that was issued a building or zoning permit during the year.

The Auditor's portal has posted tentative values for tax year 2026, payable in 2027, for owners to search by parcel. The appraisal page lists what changes a value: added square footage, additions, new outbuildings and major improvements that needed a permit. New carpet, appliances, fixtures, landscaping and a new driveway surface do not.

sections.h2: How do I appeal my Geauga County valuation?
sections.html:
Start with an informal review and hearing with one of the Auditor's appraisers, then file a formal complaint with the Board of Revision if you still disagree. The Auditor's appraisal office says an appeal needs solid evidence of at least one of three things.

  • The property record is wrong, such as a carport shown as a garage.
  • The market value is too high, and similar properties sold for less or a bank appraisal supports a lower figure.
  • The value is inequitable because similar properties are valued lower.

Under R.C. 5715.19, a complaint for the current tax year is due by March 31 of the following year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later. The Board must decide within 180 days of the last filing date. You may pay on your claimed value while the complaint is pending, and interest runs on any shortfall if you lose. A property that had a complaint in the same interim period generally cannot be challenged again unless it sold at arm's length, lost value to casualty or gained a major improvement.

sections.h2: What tax relief does Geauga County offer homeowners?
sections.html:
The Homestead Exemption shields $29,000 of a home's market value from local taxes, and the Auditor's page puts the average Geauga savings at about $518 a year. The Auditor's own example is that a $100,000 home would be billed as if it were worth $71,000.

  • Age and income: be 65 by December 31, 2026, with household income under $41,000 (2025 Ohio adjusted gross income).
  • Disability: permanently and totally disabled as of January 1, 2026 with the same income limit.
  • Veterans: a 100 percent service-connected disability rating, applying on form DTE 105I.
  • Surviving spouses: of someone who was getting the old exemption, if at least 59 when the spouse died.

File a paper application, DTE 105A, with the Auditor by December 31. Original signatures are required and the office does not take electronic filing. A denied application can be appealed to the Board of Revision on form DTE 106B. The Auditor also runs an Owner Occupancy Credit tool, the farm CAUV and forestry programs and a destroyed property deduction.

sections.h2: What if a Geauga County house is damaged or destroyed?
sections.html:
The Auditor can lower the value of real estate hurt by fire, flood, ice or other causes, but cannot issue refunds for earlier years. File the damaged property application as soon as possible. The deduction depends on the calendar quarter of the damage.

Damage from January through March earns a 100 percent deduction and April through June earns 75 percent, and the deadline for both is December 31. July through September earns 50 percent with the same deadline. October through December earns 25 percent, with a January 31 deadline. The reduction stays until the property is restored.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about taxes at a Geauga County closing?
sections.html:
Geauga County deeds go to the Auditor for transfer before they are recorded. The Auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value and $0.50 per parcel, and updates the tax records when the parcel moves.

Ask the Treasurer for the amount owed on the parcel and ask your title company how the February and July bills are being split. The Auditor's real estate page also links a Forfeited Land Sale page, which is the place to look if taxes on a parcel were missed.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Geauga County homes?
sections.html:
Geauga County had 95,397 residents in the 2020 Census. About 87.2 percent of homes are owner occupied, the median value of those homes is $331,100, and median household income is $107,860. The 2025 permit count was 180.

The county was formed in 1806, covers about 400 square miles of land and includes Chardon, Burton, Middlefield and South Russell. The Village of Aquilla was dissolved by a vote in November 2024.

faqs.q: When are Geauga County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due on the second Wednesday of February and the second Wednesday of July. Bills for the first half go out in January and for the second half in June, and the Treasurer mails them.

faqs.q: What is the Geauga County homestead exemption worth?
faqs.a: The exemption shields $29,000 of market value, and the Auditor estimates average savings of about $518 a year. You must apply on paper with the Auditor by December 31 and meet the age or disability and income rules.

faqs.q: How do I contest my Geauga County property value?
faqs.a: Ask the Auditor's appraisal office for an informal review, and if that fails, file a complaint with the Board of Revision. Ohio law sets the deadline at March 31 of the next year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

faqs.q: Does the Treasurer ever text tax bills?
faqs.a: No. The Treasurer sends bills only by regular mail. A text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent and should be deleted.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Geauga County real estate taxes?
faqs.a: Call the Auditor's real estate office at (440) 279-1617 for values, exemptions and credits. The Auditor's main number is (440) 279-1600, and the office is open from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm Monday through Friday.
